queries.query: How does the self-attention mechanism compute attention scores?
queries.gold_answer: For each token the model computes a Query (Q), a Key (K) and a Value (V) vector. The attention score between two tokens is the dot product of their Query and Key vectors, scaled by the square root of the key dimension, and the output for a position is the softmax-weighted sum of the Value vectors.

queries.query: What is the Encoder-Decoder structure of the original Transformer?
queries.gold_answer: The original Transformer consists of an encoder that maps an input sequence to continuous representations and a decoder that generates the output one symbol at a time, attending to both the encoder output and its own previous outputs. Each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention sublayer and a feed-forward sublayer; each decoder layer adds a cross-attention sublayer that attends to the encoder output.

queries.query: How are entities and relationships extracted from text in GraphRAG?
queries.gold_answer: Modern knowledge graphs are built through automated information extraction using named entity recognition, relation extraction and coreference resolution, with systems like OpenIE extracting subject-predicate-object triples at scale; LLM-based extraction identifies entity names, types and relationships in a single forward pass and often beats pipeline-based extraction on implicit relationships.
queries.note: knowledge_graphs -- Automated Extraction / LLM-Based Extraction sections

queries.query: What is Wikidata and who maintains it?
queries.gold_answer: Wikidata is a free, collaboratively edited knowledge base maintained by the Wikimedia Foundation and used as a central storage hub for structured data across the Wikimedia projects. It holds over 100 million data items, supports multiple languages, and was founded in 2012 with support from Google, Microsoft and the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence.

queries.query: What are knowledge graph embedding methods like TransE and RotatE?
queries.gold_answer: Knowledge graph embedding models represent entities and relationships as dense vectors in a continuous space. TransE, the earliest and most influential, represents a relationship as a translation so that head + relation approximately equals tail; later models include RotatE (rotations in complex space), DistMult (bilinear scoring) and ComplEx (complex-valued embeddings), supporting tasks such as link prediction and entity alignment.

queries.query: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation and why does it matter?
queries.gold_answer: RAG is a technique that grounds LLM outputs in external documents retrieved at query time; it was introduced by Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research in 2020. It combines a parametric memory (the trained weights) with a non-parametric memory (a searchable corpus), so the model first retrieves relevant passages and then answers conditioned on the question and those passages.

queries.query: How does HyDE improve retrieval quality in RAG systems?
queries.gold_answer: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) generates a hypothetical answer to the query first and then uses that as the retrieval query, which often improves recall. It is one of the pre-retrieval steps that Advanced RAG adds, alongside query rewriting, with reranking and context compression as post-retrieval steps.

queries.query: What is HNSW and how does it speed up approximate nearest neighbor search?
queries.gold_answer: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the most widely adopted approximate nearest neighbour algorithm. It builds a multi-layer graph in which each layer is a navigable small-world network; a query starts at the top layer and greedily descends to the bottom, following edges to progressively closer nodes, which gives sub-millisecond query times on million-scale datasets. IVF is the alternative: it partitions the space into Voronoi cells and searches only the nearest clusters.
queries.note: vector_databases -- Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search section

queries.query: What is Direct Preference Optimization and how does it differ from RLHF?
queries.gold_answer: DPO is a more recent alternative to RLHF that removes the explicit reward model and the RL training loop, optimising the model directly on preference pairs of chosen and rejected responses, which makes training simpler and more stable. RLHF instead has human annotators rank responses, trains a reward model from those rankings and fine-tunes the LLM with PPO.

queries.query: How is a basic retrieval-augmented pipeline put together, and which chunking and retrieval-quality problems does it face?
queries.gold_answer: The simplest RAG pipeline chunks documents into fixed-size pieces, embeds them, stores them in a vector index, retrieves the top-k at query time and passes them to the LLM; it suffers from chunking boundary issues and can miss multi-hop reasoning that requires connecting information across documents. On the quality side, chunks that are too small lose context while chunks that are too large dilute relevance signals, and dense retrieval can miss exact-match queries for named entities, IDs or rare terms, which is why hybrid dense + BM25 retrieval usually wins on mixed query types.

queries.query: How did Google's Knowledge Graph come about, and what happened to Freebase afterwards?
queries.gold_answer: Google popularised the term 'knowledge graph' in 2012 when it launched the Google Knowledge Graph to enhance search results with structured entity information; the system held over 500 million entities at launch and drew on Freebase, Wikipedia and the CIA World Factbook. Freebase itself was a large collaborative knowledge base developed by Metaweb and acquired by Google in 2010; Google shut it down in 2016 and migrated its data to Wikidata.

queries.query: How do FAISS and LanceDB differ in how they are deployed and what they support?
queries.gold_answer: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is an open-source library from Meta AI Research supporting IVF, HNSW and PQ index types; it runs entirely in-process with no server component, which suits embedded applications and research prototypes, and it does not natively support metadata filtering. LanceDB is also open-source and serverless, built on the Lance columnar format, runs in-process, supports SQL-like queries alongside vector search, and is designed for multimodal data -- Microsoft's GraphRAG uses it as its default local vector store.

required_terms: does not natively support metadata filtering

queries.query: What is a knowledge graph, and which vector store does Microsoft's GraphRAG use by default?
queries.gold_answer: A knowledge graph is a structured representation of facts about entities and the relationships between them, with typed edges such as 'founded_by' or 'works_at' that let machines reason in a structured way. The vector store side of that stack: Microsoft's GraphRAG uses LanceDB as its default local vector store -- LanceDB is an open-source, serverless vector database built on the Lance columnar format that runs in-process and supports SQL-like queries alongside vector search.

required_terms: edge carries a specific relationship type

queries.query: In what year was the Transformer architecture introduced, and in what year was the RAG paper published?
queries.gold_answer: The Transformer was introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017 in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'. The RAG paper, 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks', was published by Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research in 2020.

queries.query: How do knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation each let a search system show where an answer came from?
queries.gold_answer: With a knowledge graph, search engines show structured information panels next to the traditional results -- for a well-known person, organisation or place the engine displays structured facts such as birth date, nationality and notable works drawn straight from the graph. RAG does the same job with citations: because the answer is grounded in specific retrieved passages, the system can point to exact source documents, which improves interpretability and trustworthiness.

queries.query: In its most basic arrangement, how are materials divided, turned into numbers, and searched when someone asks -- and what limitation does that arrangement have?
queries.gold_answer: In the simplest RAG pipeline, documents are chunked into fixed-size pieces, the pieces are embedded, stored in a vector index, and the top-k are retrieved at query time and passed to the LLM. That approach suffers from chunking boundary issues and can miss multi-hop reasoning that requires connecting information across documents.

queries.query: Which later work carried this design beyond writing, and what happens to the workload once the input grows?
queries.gold_answer: The Transformer led directly to BERT for bidirectional pre-training, to T5 (every NLP task as a text-to-text problem) and to the Vision Transformer, which applied the architecture to image recognition by treating image patches as sequence tokens -- so the design was not limited to language tasks. The cost is quadratic: self-attention has quadratic complexity with respect to sequence length, which creates challenges for very long sequences, which is why sparse or approximate variants such as Longformer, BigBird and Linformer were proposed.
queries.note: paraphrase of the Impact and Successors passage; the query shares no stemmed content word with the gold chunk

queries.query: When one technique copes with codes and the second copes with meaning, how can the two be merged so that neither blind spot dominates?
queries.gold_answer: Pure vector search retrieves semantically similar documents but can miss exact-match queries for named entities, identifiers or rare terms, while pure keyword search (BM25/TF-IDF) handles exact matches well but fails on semantic or paraphrase queries. Hybrid search combines both signals to outperform either approach alone on mixed query types, either by Reciprocal Rank Fusion -- summing reciprocal ranks from several ranked lists -- or by weighted fusion, which assigns explicit weights to each signal and combines the normalised scores linearly.
